supporting_cards.title: Build the five core SMS flows (welcome + four abandonments + post-purchase)
supporting_cards.summary: Every brand should run a welcome flow, site/browse/cart/checkout abandonment, and a post-purchase replenishment or win-back flow.
supporting_cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing the automated (flow) side of an SMS program.
steps: Welcome flow: triggered when someone joins via the popup (often with a discount). Keep it simple — introduce the brand and drive the discount.

Four abandonment flows, kept dead simple: site abandoned (browsed site, no product page), browse abandoned (viewed a product page), cart abandoned (added to cart), checkout abandoned (reached checkout).
Post-purchase / replenishment / win-back flow: bring buyers back after their first order.
Keep abandonment messages single and simple (see the US compliance card) and split by new vs. returning buyers when you can.

Treat these basics as the moneymakers: the source reports one brand's core flows producing $517k, with $293k from welcome, $107k cart abandoned, $46k browse abandoned, $20k retention, and $13k site abandoned in a month.
caveats: Revenue figures are a single agency portfolio example, not a benchmark to expect.
Exact flow structure should be adjusted per brand context.
supporting_cards.source_name: How to Create a SMS Marketing Strategy For $10M Shopify Brands.docx

supporting_cards.title: Keep only high-engagement flows during recovery
supporting_cards.summary: Pause most automations and lean on welcome, abandon and post-purchase flows, which reliably earn high engagement.
supporting_cards.use_when: Deciding which automations to leave running while rebuilding sender reputation, or which flows to prioritize when you can't build everything at once.
steps: Turn off all flows except: welcome, browse abandonment, cart abandonment, checkout abandonment and post-purchase.
Keep the welcome flow because contacts just opted in for a discount and will open the first email delivering it.
Keep cart and checkout abandonment because the reminder about an item they were already considering earns strong engagement.
Keep post-purchase because customers want order information.
Understand why this matters during recovery: every send that gets opens and clicks is a vote of confidence with providers; flows generate those votes without needing new campaign content.
Re-enable the remaining flows once engagement and placement have recovered.
caveats: This is the source's recommended recovery posture, not a claim that other flows are worthless.
If a flow's own engagement is weak for your brand, including it dilutes the signal you're trying to send.

supporting_cards.title: Have the Five Core Flows Plus Win-Back and Sunset in Place
supporting_cards.summary: Prioritize the essential lifecycle flows the source calls the biggest money-makers: welcome series, site abandon, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon, post-purchase, win-back, and sunset.
supporting_cards.use_when: Auditing which automation flows a store still needs, or sequencing which flows to build first.
steps: Confirm the pre-purchase set exists: welcome series, site abandon, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon.
Confirm post-purchase and customer win-back exist as post-purchase flows.
Confirm the sunset flow exists for list hygiene.
The source singles out the welcome series, cart abandon, and browse abandon as the most important flows to keep optimizing over time — treat them as ongoing optimization targets, not set-and-forget.

Beyond the core, the source lists optional/extended flows as the possibilities are 'endless': bounceback offer right after purchase, back-in-stock, replacement reminder (e.g., a 30-day consumable prompted at ~day 25), product/data-based cross-sell flows, and a tailored 'highly engaged but never purchased' window-shopper flow.
caveats: Which flows are 'biggest money-makers' is the presenter's assessment, not a measured benchmark across stores.
Build order should consider your data volume — some flows (e.g., back-in-stock) need inventory/restock events to exist.

supporting_cards.title: Split subject line and preview text to stay readable on mobile
supporting_cards.summary: Short subject lines plus a complementary preview text raise the chance the whole first impression is read on a small screen.
supporting_cards.use_when: Writing campaign subject lines and preheaders for a store's promotions or content sends.
steps: Treat the subject line's only job as getting the open; it must create curiosity or intrigue and stand out in a crowded inbox.
Treat the preview text as a second subject line — many brands skip or waste it by focusing only on the subject line.
Follow up on the subject line's promise in the preview text and tease the content without lying; a high open rate from a broken promise leads to spam complaints or unsubscribes.

Avoid full sentences: use a few words in the subject line and a few in the preview text. Because most opens happen on mobile, a long subject line is cut off — split one long idea between the two fields.
Do not promise in subject/preview what the email doesn't deliver.
caveats: The segment cuts off after listing the email's headline; exact character limits are not specified in the source.
Open rates are not the only goal — delivering the promise protects sender reputation.

supporting_cards.title: Upload a finished image-design email into an ESP as stacked images
supporting_cards.summary: Set up a campaign, strip the template, upload compressed slices in order, remove padding, add links, then test and send.
supporting_cards.use_when: Publishing an image-based email built in Figma into Omnisend, Klaviyo or a similar platform.
steps: Create the campaign in the ESP, entering the subject line and preheader text (the presenter uses 'Last chance for 20% off' with preheader 'Open for your last gift opportunity').
Open any template to get a canvas, then delete the template blocks so you start from an empty email.
Add image elements one by one and upload your compressed slices, stacking them in the exact order they appear in the design.
Select each image block and remove image padding plus any frame side padding so the stacked slices align edge to edge and look like one continuous design.
Assign the destination link for each image — one link per image — and add short alt text describing the image.
Preview and send a test email to your own address, checking that the unsubscribe link is present (the ESP added one automatically in the walkthrough) and that links and rendering are correct.
Choose recipients — all subscribers or a specific segment with exclusions — review, then send.
caveats: Omnisend and other ESP interfaces change frequently; verify current campaign, padding and image-upload controls.
Sending entirely image-based emails means text-only recipients see alt text, so keep alt text meaningful.
supporting_cards.source_name: How to Design High Converting Ecommerce Emails In Figma.docx

supporting_cards.title: Clear and concise email copy: short and sweet, one takeaway
supporting_cards.summary: Keep emails to one to two scrolls and one clear takeaway; assume readers are overwhelmed and forget multiple points.
supporting_cards.use_when: Writing campaign or flow copy that risks cramming several benefits or messages into one send.
steps: Keep the email to roughly 1-2 phone scrolls maximum; source's guidance is shorter is better because only a few seconds of attention are available.
Choose ONE takeaway per email and build the headline around it — e.g. a matcha email solely about 'enhances the benefits of caffeine', or a hair-loss email solely about growth potential.
Ask yourself before sending: is there one clear thing the customer can take away? If the email tries to give 3+ takeaways, assume readers remember none.
Split a benefit-stuffed email into a series: instead of one email listing estimator, graphs, alerts, multi-cook view, etc., dedicate a whole email to each feature one at a time.

Cut implied information. On a welcome email, skip telling subscribers they get exclusive offers/insider access (they already know from the opt-in) and let the discount code sit in the clear space you save.
Every sentence should move the reader toward a purchase; delete fluff that only fills space.
caveats: Some emails (e.g. a flowchart or comparison email) are intentionally longer because the format itself is the engagement — length alone isn't the failure, unclear/multi-message copy is.

supporting_cards.title: Treat deliverability as a sender reputation score
supporting_cards.summary: Inbox providers rank you like a credit score: good reputation lands in primary, bad lands in spam, mediocre lands in promotions.
supporting_cards.use_when: When diagnosing why campaigns aren't being seen, or when deciding whether low revenue is a content problem or a placement problem.
steps: Frame deliverability as your domain/IP 'credit score' — the question is whether you land in primary, promotions or spam.
Understand the provider's incentive: inbox providers only surface emails users want so users keep using the platform; they watch engagement as the signal.
Use open and click engagement as the practical proxy: if few people open or click, providers push you toward promotions or spam, which further reduces visibility — a self-reinforcing cycle.
Check the technical layer first: the source says if your ESP (e.g., Klaviyo) shows no warning at the top of the homepage about domain setup, assume technical requirements are already in place.
If technicals are fine, split the cause into two: either your emails are weak, or your sender reputation is poor and you are being filtered.
caveats: The credit-score framing is the source's analogy, not an official metric.
The source's claim that a clean ESP dashboard means you're fine is a simplification — authentication and domain setup still deserve a direct check.

supporting_cards.title: Maintain sender reputation with bounce, spam and engagement thresholds
supporting_cards.summary: Treat sender reputation like a credit score and monitor the three inputs — bounce rate, spam complaints and engagement — against the source's thresholds.
supporting_cards.use_when: Ongoing deliverability monitoring, or when opens collapse and you need to diagnose reputation damage.
steps: Understand the model: reputation is history-based and hard to rebuild once damaged; a good reputation gets primary inbox placement, a bad one gets spam or promotions tab.

Keep bounce rate under 1%. Bounces come from invalid addresses — e.g. a fake email submitted through a pop-up form still triggering the welcome or abandoned-cart flow. Suppress hard-bouncing addresses and consider preventing obviously fake form entries.

Keep spam complaint rate below 0.3%, and ideally below 0.1%, to stay inside Gmail and Yahoo's stricter 2024+ requirements. Locate these rates in your account reporting and review on a regular cadence.
Maximise positive engagement signals: opens, clicks and especially replies tell inbox providers people want to hear from you. Low opens and low clicks act as negative signals.
Send at a consistent cadence — the source cites an example of two campaigns a week plus flows sending daily — because erratic sending (long silence then a burst) is treated as a negative signal.
Fix the root cause before re-sending: low opens usually means wrong audience (see 180-day cleaning and engagement segments), not a subject-line problem.
caveats: Thresholds (0.3% complaint, 0.1% ideal, 1% bounce) are the source's targets and align with stated Gmail/Yahoo expectations; Google's published requirements should be checked for current limits.
Reputation damage is slow to reverse, so prevention, not remediation, is the practical strategy.
supporting_cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

supporting_cards.title: Deliverability Hygiene: Authentication, Engagement Tiers and List Cleaning
supporting_cards.summary: Implement SPF, DKIM and DMARC, segment by engagement recency, and suppress long-inactive subscribers to protect inbox placement.
supporting_cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing sending infrastructure and list health, especially before scaling campaign volume.
steps: Implement the technical authentication trio — SPF, DKIM and DMARC — on your sending domain so mailbox providers can verify you.
Segment by engagement recency using activity windows; the source names 14-day, 30-day, 60-day and 90-day active tiers as the segmentation structure.
Use those tiers to differentiate sending: mail the most recently engaged tiers most often and reduce frequency or exclude the least engaged tiers.
Clean the list by suppressing profiles that have been inactive past 180 days — the source's stated list-cleaning benchmark.
Monitor inbox placement and sender reputation, particularly as AI-driven inbox curation changes how mail is sorted and surfaced.
Re-check authentication records and suppression rules after any change of sending domain, ESP or marketing platform.
caveats: The 180-day suppression threshold and the 14/30/60/90-day windows are the source's heuristics, not calculations derived from your data — adjust for your purchase cycle and list size.
Suppressing inactive profiles reduces list size and can reduce short-term revenue; the source frames it as necessary for placement.
Authentication setup depends on your DNS provider and ESP interface, both of which change — verify current configuration steps.

foundation_candidates.title: Employ retention and account-level setup: where email sits in the 2026 lifecycle
foundation_candidates.summary: Commit to a measured email cadence and a five-flow automated core, then extend with gamification, zero-party-data quizzes and split desktop/mobile experiences.
foundation_candidates.use_when: Roadmapping the lifecycle programme, deciding sending frequency, and prioritising which automations to build first.
steps: Set the base sending cadence at 3–4 campaigns per week, the source's recommended campaign frequency. Consistency matters as much as volume for reputation — erratic bursts are a negative signal.
Prioritise the five core Klaviyo automated flows: Welcome, Browse Abandonment, Abandoned Cart, Abandoned Checkout and Post-Purchase. These are the standard set to build before advanced work.
Give the welcome flow a fast clock: the first 72 hours after signup is the critical conversion window, with day zero driving the highest purchase volume. Put your best converting email first.

After the core is in place, add advanced tactics the source lists: active gamification such as spin-to-win or scratch-off capture, zero-party data collection quizzes, and separate split-tested desktop and mobile experiences rather than one responsive template.

Recognise that the inbox itself is now AI-curated (e.g. Gmail's AI inbox), so authentication, regular cleaning and engagement-tiered segmentation are the levers that put mail in the primary inbox rather than the promotions tab.
Track cadence, flow coverage and inbox placement as programme health metrics, and be prepared to iterate rather than set and forget.
caveats: 3–4 campaigns per week plus flow volume is aggressive for some audiences; the source also tells you to learn whether emails are wanted, so cadence should be validated against engagement and spam complaints.
The 72-hour welcome window and day-zero concentration are the source's observations across an agency portfolio, not a guarantee for every offer type.
